chapters.title: Computer
chapters.blurb: What's inside the box, what runs on it, and how you talk to it — the foundation every other chapter sits on.

blocks.h: A device that receives input, processes it, then produces output.

blocks.ins: Type a calculation and follow the data through input, process and output.

kids: Any program or set of instructions

blocks.h: Learn the one-line difference: hardware = touch it, software = instructions. It is a classic 1-mark question.
The physical components that make up a computer system.

kids: Sound card — audio in and out
Internal HDD / SSD — stores OS and files

blocks.r: The monitor is external — you can see it from outside. The GPU that drives it is internal.

blocks.h: Hardware that processes instructions to produce an output.

kids: Fetches, decodes and manages execution of instructions

blocks.h: Use the verbs: CU = controls / manages, ALU = calculates and decides.

blocks.r: The CPU processes data. Storing is the job of memory and storage.

blocks.h: Internal memory directly accessible by the CPU. Also called primary or internal memory.

kids: Stores instructions, software, data and OS parts currently in use

blocks.title: Does it survive a power cut?

RAM
ROM

blocks.h: A program that carries out a hardware check to find out whether all devices are present and functional.

blocks.title: Backing storage
items: Files, software, moving data to another computer

blocks.h: Asked to explain "volatile"? Say: contents are lost when power is turned off. Always link it to power.

blocks.w: "RAM is permanent storage" or "ROM is temporary".
blocks.r: RAM = volatile, temporary. ROM = non-volatile, permanent. Never swap them.

blocks.q: Your laptop loses an unsaved document in a power cut. Which memory held it?
blocks.a: RAM — it's volatile, so everything in it vanishes without power.

blocks.h: Programs for controlling the operation of a computer and for processing electronic data.

blocks.title: System software, explained
head: Software
What it does
rows: Lets hardware devices communicate with the OS
Translates high-level code into computer language
Combines modules into a single program

blocks.title: Compiler: from source code to object code
blocks.ins: Press Replay and watch source code become machine code the CPU can run.

blocks.title: Linker: many object files, one program
blocks.ins: Press Replay to see several object files combine into one program.

blocks.r: Antivirus is a utility, so it is system software.

blocks.h: System software that lets the user communicate with the hardware and perform many basic tasks.

blocks.title: Functions of the OS
items: Lets you interact with the computer

blocks.h: "Describe OS functions" = give 3 different ones from the list. Do not repeat one in different words.

tabs.d: Command Line Interface — the user types commands to interact with the computer.
p: Uses less memory than a GUI
c: Commands must be learned and memorised

tabs.d: Graphical User Interface — built around graphical items, using the WIMP system.
p: Pointer and icons are quicker than typing
c: Limited to the icons and menus provided
Settings are protected from the user

tabs.d: Dialogue-based (voice) interface — speech recognition; spoken words carry out actions.
c: Must be trained; limited commands stored

tabs.d: Gesture-based interface — the body gives commands without keyboard or mouse, using computer vision and image processing.
c: Only works near the camera or sensor
Gestures must be learned; may exclude users with physical disabilities

blocks.h: For each of CLI, GUI, Dialogue-based and Gesture-based, know the definition + 2 advantages + 2 disadvantages.

blocks.w: "GUI is easier" or "CLI is faster" — with no reason.
blocks.r: Give the reason: GUI needs no commands memorised; CLI uses less memory and processing power.

tabs.d: Desktop — large, non-portable computer designed to sit on a desk. Uses: office, education, gaming, entertainment.
c: Needs constant power — no use in a power cut

tabs.d: Laptop — portable, battery-powered, with built-in keyboard, screen and touchpad.
c: More expensive than a similar desktop

tabs.d: Tablet — touchscreen portable device with no physical keyboard (optional external one).
c: Typing on a touchscreen is slower

tabs.d: Smartphone — handheld device combining phone, internet, camera, GPS and computing. The most portable computer.
p: Easy to use on the move

tabs.d: Phablet — a tablet that works as a smartphone; size sits between the two.
p: Makes phone calls like a smartphone
c: Bigger to carry than a phone

blocks.h: There are 5 types: PC (desktop), laptop, tablet, smartphone, phablet. The last four are mobile computers.

blocks.w: "Laptops are better because they are portable."
blocks.r: Always compare: portable compared to a desktop. A smartphone is more portable still. Name both sides.

blocks.q: Which device can be used during a power cut and is easy to upgrade?
blocks.a: Trick question — no single one. A desktop is easy to upgrade but needs constant power; mobile devices have batteries but are often hard to upgrade.

quiz.t: Which of these is an example of hardware?
quiz.e: Hardware is anything you can physically touch. The others are software.

quiz.t: Which part of the CPU performs calculations and logical decisions?
quiz.e: The ALU does arithmetic and comparisons. The Control Unit manages instructions.

quiz.t: A computer loses unsaved work when power is cut. This is because RAM is…
quiz.e: Volatile means contents are lost when power is switched off.

quiz.t: What does the BIOS do when a computer starts?
o: Checks that hardware devices are present and working
quiz.e: BIOS is stored in ROM and performs a hardware check at start-up.

quiz.t: Which statement about backing storage is correct?
o: Slower to access than main memory
quiz.e: Backing storage is non-volatile and not directly accessed by the CPU, so it is slower.

quiz.t: Which of the following is system software?
quiz.e: Utilities help maintain the computer, making them system software.

quiz.t: Which is NOT a function of an operating system?
quiz.e: Image editing is a job for application software.

quiz.t: Which is an advantage of a CLI over a GUI?
o: Uses less memory and processing power
quiz.e: CLI needs no graphics, so it uses less memory and processing power.

quiz.t: What does the P in WIMP stand for?
quiz.e: WIMP = Windows, Icons, Menus, Pointer.

quiz.t: Which is a disadvantage of a desktop compared with a laptop?
o: Cannot be used during a power cut
quiz.e: A desktop has no built-in battery, so it needs constant power.

chapters.title: Input
chapters.blurb: How data gets into a computer — from a mouse click to a contactless payment.

blocks.h: A device that sends data to a computer for processing, turning input into a form the computer can understand. Under the control of the user.

kids: Must be converted to be processed
Temperature, sound, light, weight, human voice

blocks.h: ADC converts analogue to digital so a computer can read it. DAC converts digital to analogue — to control an external device or send to an actuator.
Remember the letters: Analogue-to-Digital goes in (microphone); Digital-to-Analogue goes out (speaker).

blocks.w: "A computer can process analogue data directly."
blocks.r: Computers only process digital data. Analogue must pass through an ADC first.

blocks.h: A device used to move and control the on-screen pointer (cursor).

tabs.u: Moving the pointer · opening, closing, minimising software · moving and deleting files
p: Needs less desk area than a keyboard
Faster way to choose an option than a keyboard
c: Hard for people with restricted hand/wrist movement

tabs.u: Moving the pointer · opening, closing, minimising software · moving and deleting files
p: Faster than a keyboard for choosing options
Takes less space than a mouse
c: Harder to control than a mouse

tabs.u: Alternative to a mouse for restricted hand/wrist movement · some luxury cars
p: More accurate pointer than a mouse

tabs.u: Racing and flying games · simulators · remote control of drones and vehicles
p: Easier than a keyboard to navigate
c: Harder to control a pointer than other devices

tabs.d: Like a joystick, used whenever steering is required.
tabs.u: Video games · simulators
p: Easier than keyboard or joystick for steering
c: More expensive than a mouse or joystick
Steering can be too sensitive — unrealistic feel

tabs.u: Inputting freehand drawings
p: More accurate for drawing than other pointing devices

tabs.u: TVs, projectors and home appliances from a distance
p: Useful for people with walking difficulties

blocks.r: A touchscreen is an input AND output device — it is not a pointing device.

tabs.u: Inputting data into applications · typing commands
c: Must learn to type for speed

tabs.u: ATMs (PIN) · POS terminals if the barcode fails · Chip and PIN devices · numeric data in spreadsheets
c: Small keys can make input difficult

blocks.title: How a keyboard works
blocks.ins: Tap a key (or type one) and follow the signal from the circuit board to the CPU.

blocks.h: Numeric keypad uses: remember ATM, POS, Chip and PIN — anywhere numbers are typed fast.
Devices that input data with minimal human interaction. Faster than typing, and errors are reduced (no manual input).

tabs.d: Optical Mark Reader — reads the position of marks on hard-copy forms.
tabs.u: Multiple-choice exam papers · school registers · surveys · lottery tickets
p: Fast for large amounts of data
c: Cannot recognise printed or handwritten characters
Marks must be in a specific area
Faint marks may not be read
Forms may need manual checks — slow and costly

tabs.d: Optical Character Reader — scans text from a hard-copy document and converts it to digital text.
tabs.u: Passports and ID cards · digitising documents · number plate recognition (ANPR)
p: More accurate than OMR for detailed data

tabs.d: Barcode — black and white lines of varying thickness representing digits or characters. A barcode reader scans them.
tabs.u: Supermarket checkouts · automatic stock control · library loans
c: Must be close to the barcode

tabs.d: QR code — a matrix of black and white squares that can link to websites, videos or text. Three big corner squares help alignment.
tabs.u: Advertising · linking to email, website or phone number · electronic boarding passes
p: Holds more data than a barcode
Any camera device can scan it
Faster to scan; can be small
c: Can be used to transmit malicious code
More than one QR format exists

tabs.d: RFID reader — reads RFID tags using radio waves, with no contact or line-of-sight. A tag has a microchip (stores data) and an antenna (receives/transmits).
tabs.u: Stock control · tracking livestock · libraries · passports (biometrics) · car parks · contactless payment · access cards

blocks.title: How a QR code is read
steps: Aim the phone camera at the code
The app converts squares into data

tabs.d: Magnetic stripe reader — reads the stripe on a card (credit/debit, hotel key).
p: Faster than manual entry; fewer errors
c: No PIN needed — less secure if lost
Does not work at a distance

tabs.d: Chip and PIN reader — compares the PIN entered with the PIN stored on the chip.
c: Typing a PIN risks shoulder surfing
Does not work at a distance

tabs.d: Contactless / NFC reader — reads a card or phone held close, using Near Field Communication. No PIN for small amounts.
c: Can be read accidentally or from a distance

blocks.h: DDE advantages always come in a pair: faster than typing and fewer errors. Say both.

blocks.w: "Chip and PIN is less secure than a magnetic stripe."
blocks.r: Chip and PIN is more secure — the PIN must match the chip, and the chip data is encrypted.

blocks.q: Which DDE device marks multiple-choice exam papers?
blocks.a: An OMR — it reads the position of marks on the form.

tabs.u: Photography · scanning documents · security cameras
c: Resolution not as good as expensive traditional cameras

tabs.u: Video conferencing · security recording · streaming
Converting documents and photographs to digital format

blocks.h: Inputs sound or voice into a computer. It uses an ADC to convert analogue sound waves into digital data.

tabs.u: Speech in presentations · voice-activation systems · speech-to-text software
c: Sound files use a lot of memory
Speech recognition is prone to errors

blocks.h: An input AND output device — input by touching the screen with a finger or stylus. It is not a pointing device.

tabs.u: ATMs · public information systems · phones, tablets and phablets
c: Screen gets dirty and less responsive

tabs.u: Selecting objects and drawing on CRT screens (CAD)
p: Small — good where space is tight

blocks.r: Light pens only work with CRT monitors — one reason the technology is outdated.

quiz.t: Which device converts analogue sound from a microphone into data a computer can process?
quiz.e: An ADC converts analogue to digital.

quiz.t: Which is an example of analogue data?
quiz.e: Natural variables such as temperature, sound and light are analogue.

quiz.t: Which is classed as a pointing device?
quiz.e: A touchscreen is input AND output but not a pointing device. A tracker ball is.

quiz.t: Which is a disadvantage of a graphics tablet?
o: More expensive than other pointing devices
quiz.e: Graphics tablets are accurate for drawing but cost more.

quiz.t: Where is a numeric keypad commonly used?
o: Entering a PIN at an ATM
quiz.e: Keypads are used in ATMs, POS terminals and Chip and PIN devices.

quiz.t: Which device reads the position of marks on a multiple-choice paper?
quiz.e: OMR reads the position of marks on forms.

quiz.t: Which is an advantage of QR codes over barcodes?
o: They must be aligned to scan
They can be read from many angles
quiz.e: QR codes hold more data and can be read from any angle by any camera device.

quiz.t: An RFID tag is made of…
quiz.e: A microchip stores data; an antenna receives and transmits it.

quiz.t: Why is Chip and PIN more secure than a magnetic stripe?
o: The PIN must match the data on the chip
quiz.e: The entered PIN is compared with the PIN stored (encrypted) on the chip.

quiz.t: Which input device only works with CRT monitors?
quiz.e: Light pens only work with CRT screens.

chapters.title: Output
chapters.blurb: How a computer shows, prints, plays and moves the results of its work.

blocks.h: A device that receives data from the computer and displays the results of processed data.

blocks.title: Input vs output
head: Input devices
Output devices
rows: Send data to a computer for processing
Turn input into a form the computer understands
Display the results of processed data
Under the control of the user
Under the control of the computer

blocks.h: Who is in control? Input = the user. Output = the computer. That one line earns the mark.

tabs.d: Cathode Ray Tube — the oldest type, large and bulky, uses an electron beam to display images.
tabs.u: Specialist areas such as CAD · used with light pens
p: Wider viewing angle than most LCDs

tabs.d: Liquid Crystal Display — thin, flat screen using liquid crystals and a backlight. Often called TFT.
tabs.u: Main output device of modern computers · phones, tablets, laptops, portable games · many offer touch input

tabs.d: Light Emitting Diode — uses LEDs as the backlight instead of the fluorescent tubes in LCD. Newest display technology.

blocks.w: "LED monitors use LEDs to make the picture instead of liquid crystals."
blocks.r: LED monitors still use an LCD panel. The LEDs are the backlight, replacing the fluorescent tubes.

tabs.d: Uses static electricity and toner (powder). A non-impact printer.
tabs.u: Offices needing low noise · fast, high-quality, high-volume printing
c: Coloured laser has high running cost

tabs.d: Uses liquid ink (thermal bubble or piezoelectric). A non-impact printer.
tabs.u: Low output volumes · printing photographs · inkjet technology is also used in 3D printing
c: High running cost — ink runs out fast

tabs.d: Uses a matrix of pins and an inked ribbon. The only impact printer here.
tabs.u: Noisy or dirty places (garage workshops) · quality not important · carbon copies (wage slips) · till receipts
p: Best in dusty or dirty places

tabs.d: Produces solid 3D objects.
tabs.u: Prototypes · customised items (prosthetic limbs that fit exactly, surgical equipment) · parts for items no longer in production
p: Easier and faster to make customised items
Can make parts no longer produced
Medical uses: organs, prosthetics, tissue engineering

tabs.d: Uses pens to produce large, very high quality drawings and diagrams.
tabs.u: Architectural and engineering drawings · blueprints · cartoon characters · technical design drawings
p: Prints on many materials (aluminium, cardboard, plastic, steel, wood)

kids: Dot matrix — pins strike an inked ribbon

blocks.h: The cost of operating a device (ink, toner, ribbon, power) — different from the initial price to buy it.

blocks.title: Two inkjet mechanisms
items: Heat vaporises ink into a bubble that pushes ink out
A crystal vibrates to push ink out of the nozzle

blocks.title: How thermal inkjet works
steps: Ink is heated and vaporises into a bubble
The bubble is pushed through a nozzle onto the paper
The bubble collapses, creating a vacuum
The vacuum draws more ink from the cartridge

blocks.title: How a 3D printer builds an object
steps: Make a 3D model in CAD software
Software slices the model into layers

blocks.title: 3D printer: Additive (Direct and Binder)
blocks.ins: Switch between Direct, Binder and Subtractive to compare how each builds an object.

blocks.title: Laser vs inkjet vs dot matrix
head: Laser
Inkjet
Dot matrix

blocks.title: Which printer for which job?
head: Printer
Used when…
rows: Low noise is needed (office) · fast, high-quality, high-volume printing
Low volumes · photographs · inkjet technology is used in 3D printing
Noisy or dirty places (garage workshops) · quality not important · carbon copies (wage slips) · till receipts
Prototypes · customised items (prosthetic limbs, surgical equipment) · parts no longer in production

blocks.h: Running cost = cost of operating the device (ink, toner, ribbon). Initial cost = the price to buy it. Do not mix the two up.

blocks.w: "Laser printers are cheapest because they have the lowest running cost."
blocks.r: Laser has the highest initial cost. Be specific: low running cost per page for B&W, but high for colour.

blocks.q: Which printer can produce carbon copies?
blocks.a: The dot matrix printer — it is an impact printer, so the pins strike through multi-part paper.

blocks.h: Projects an image onto a large surface such as a screen or wall.

tabs.u: Training presentations and meetings · advertising · home cinema
p: Many people see a presentation at once

blocks.h: Convert digital audio data (via a DAC) into analogue sound waves that humans can hear.

blocks.title: How speakers work
steps: Electric current flows through a coil around an iron core
Changing current makes the core vibrate
A thin paper cone attached to the core vibrates

blocks.title: Inside a speaker
blocks.ins: Press play and watch how electrical signals become sound.

tabs.u: Phones and computers · multimedia presentations · reading text aloud for visually impaired users · playing sound files
p: Much louder than the original sound
c: Can disturb others in an office

blocks.h: A mechanical output device that produces movement — rotate, close, push or pull an object.

blocks.title: Build the circuit: drag an actuator in
blocks.ins: Drag an actuator into the circuit and switch it on.

tabs.u: Robot arm · spinning a fan · pumping water · washing machines · greenhouses (windows, fans)
p: Remote operation (e.g. nuclear reactor pumps) — big safety factor
c: Usually analogue, so computer signals need a DAC

blocks.r: An actuator is an output device — it receives a signal and produces movement.

quiz.t: Output devices are under the control of…
quiz.e: Input devices are under user control; output devices under computer control.

quiz.t: Which monitor can flicker and cause headaches?
quiz.e: CRT monitors can flicker, leading to headaches and eyestrain.

quiz.t: In an LED monitor, the LEDs are used as…
quiz.e: LEDs replace the fluorescent tubes as the backlight source.

quiz.t: Which printer is an impact printer?
quiz.e: Dot matrix uses pins against an inked ribbon. The others are non-impact.

quiz.t: Which printer is best for producing carbon copies?
quiz.e: Dot matrix can print multi-part and carbon copies.

quiz.t: What is the first step in 3D printing?
quiz.e: A 3D model is made in CAD and imported, then sliced into layers.

quiz.t: Which is a disadvantage of inkjet printers?
quiz.e: Ink cartridges run out quickly and ink is expensive.

quiz.t: What is an advantage of a multimedia projector?
o: Many people can view at once
quiz.e: It lets many people see a presentation instead of crowding round a screen.

quiz.t: What converts digital audio data to analogue before the speaker?
quiz.e: The DAC converts digital to analogue; the speaker turns it into sound.

quiz.t: Why do computers need a DAC to control an actuator?
quiz.e: Actuators are usually analogue, so the computer’s digital signal must be converted.

chapters.title: Storage
chapters.blurb: Where data lives when the power is off — and how to choose the right place for it.

blocks.h: Non-volatile storage that stores data permanently. Not directly accessed by the CPU, so slower than main memory.

Definition
Speed

Data accessed directly without passing other files

Hardware that reads or writes the media — e.g. a DVD drive

blocks.r: A CD is storage media. The device is the CD drive that reads or writes it.

tabs.u: Storing the OS · system software and working files · real-time systems · file servers

tabs.d: Portable hard disk drive — an external magnetic drive.
tabs.u: Storing backups · transferring large amounts of data between computers
c: Transfer rate not as fast as fixed HDD

tabs.d: Magnetic tape drive — accesses data serially. Very high capacity, very slow access.
tabs.u: Backups of large databases · long-term archiving

blocks.ins: Step through a read: platters spin, the arm moves, the head reads the data.

blocks.h: Tape = serial access. That single fact explains both its slow access and why it suits backups and archives.

blocks.r: Fast except magnetic tape, which accesses data serially and is very slow.

blocks.h: All optical media use laser light to read and write data.

blocks.title: How a CD is read
blocks.ins: Watch the laser read the pits and lands on a disc.

blocks.title: CD and DVD types
head: Type
Read?
Write?
Notes

Cheaper than RW; once burned behaves like ROM

tabs.u: Backups · file transfer between computers

c: More expensive than other CDs (and DVDs of the same capacity)

blocks.h: Adding data to an optical disc.

blocks.h: A storage device with no moving parts that uses flash memory chips. Any solid-state device can be called a flash drive.

tabs.d: SSD vs HDD — an SSD beats an HDD in most ways except price and capacity.
tabs.u: OS · system software and working files · real-time systems · main storage in phones and tablets
p: No moving parts — more reliable, shock-proof

tabs.d: Flash memory cards and pen drives — small removable solid-state storage.
tabs.u: Backups and file transfer · photos in cameras · phone memory cards · MP3 players · DVRs, tablets, smartphones
c: More expensive per unit than HDDs
Not all computers have card readers

blocks.title: Error messages when saving to a memory card
Magnetic vs optical vs solid-state
head: Magnetic
Optical
Solid-state
rows: Vulnerable to shock and magnetic fields

blocks.r: SSDs have no moving parts — that is why they are faster, quieter, cooler and shock-proof.

blocks.q: A photographer wants to carry hundreds of photos on a durable, tiny device. Which type of storage?
blocks.a: Solid-state — a flash memory card is compact, robust, and not affected by magnetic fields.

blocks.h: An online storage platform where data is kept at a remote location on hundreds of interlinked data servers.

kids: Controlled by one company for its employees
A mix of public and private

blocks.title: How data is stored in the cloud
steps: Use the internet from any device
Send files to a data server
Monthly or annual fee for the space used

blocks.title: How cloud data is managed
items: Server is managed by the cloud provider
If one server fails, others take over

tabs.d: Compared to storing data locally.
p: Accessible anytime, anywhere, any device (with internet)
More storage; capacity grows without new devices
Pay only for what you use
No device to carry or lose
c: Relies on provider to maintain hardware
May be less secure — many copies kept long-term
Servers damaged by disasters can lose data

blocks.h: The two security disadvantages: loss of control and multiple copies stored for a long time.

blocks.r: You need an internet connection to upload or download — the biggest disadvantage compared to local storage.

blocks.h: A copy of data stored on an alternative device as a precaution against data loss on the main storage.

blocks.title: Why back up?
items: Data on main storage can be corrupted

blocks.title: Good practice
items: Keep the backup apart from the original
Store a copy in another location
Magnetic tape is commonly used for large-scale backups

blocks.w: "Saving the file twice on the same drive is a backup."
blocks.r: A backup must be on a separate device or off-site — otherwise one failure destroys both copies.

quiz.t: Which describes serial (sequential) access?
o: Files are accessed one by one
quiz.e: Serial access passes through every file to reach the target.

quiz.t: A DVD drive is an example of…
quiz.e: The drive reads/writes the disc. The disc is the media.

quiz.t: Which storage is best for long-term archiving of large databases?
quiz.e: Tape has huge capacity and is cheap per unit, ideal for backups and archives.

quiz.t: Why is magnetic tape slow to access?
quiz.e: Data must be read one file after another.

quiz.t: Which optical disc uses a blue laser?
quiz.e: Blu-ray uses a blue laser (405 nm).

quiz.t: A CD-R can be written…
quiz.e: R disks can be written once, then behave like ROM.

quiz.t: Which is an advantage of an SSD over an HDD?
o: No moving parts, so more reliable
quiz.e: SSDs have no moving parts, making them reliable and shock-resistant.

quiz.t: Which storage type has the highest price per GB?
quiz.e: Solid-state is fastest but costs the most per GB.

quiz.t: Which is a disadvantage of cloud storage?
o: Pay only for what you use
quiz.e: Without an internet connection you lose access to your data.

quiz.t: Where should a backup be kept?
o: On a separate device or off-site
quiz.e: A separate device or off-site location protects against losing both copies.

tabs.d: Flat-file database — all data is held in a single table, with no other tables linked.
p: Easier to sort and filter data
c: Data duplication — same data in multiple records
More difficult to keep data consistent

tabs.d: Relational database — more than one table linked to each other, using relationships and a foreign key.
p: No duplication, so less data entry
Fewer errors, saves time and storage
Easier to add / modify / delete data
Better security — tables can be restricted
c: Takes more time to set up

Many records in A match many in B

blocks.h: Asked how to link two tables? The primary key of one table appears as a foreign key in the other.

blocks.r: The primary key must be unique. A foreign key can be repeated and can be null.
